document_metadata.document_title: Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual (EMC 16.20 / IDEM reference)

design_criteria.water_quality_volume_method: Treat at least one-half inch of storm water runoff (water quality volume or storage) from impervious surfaces, targeting ≥80% TSS removal on an annual average basis; post-development peak discharge rates and volumes should not exceed predevelopment levels (Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual / IDEM).
approved_bmp_categories: Pervious Concrete / Porous Asphalt / Porous Pavers

evidence.excerpt: Evansville Municipal Code Title 16 Drainage cites Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual
Treat at least one-half inch of storm water runoff (water quality volume or storage) from impervious surfaces
Water Quality Volume (WQV). The volume of runoff generated by one inch of rainfall on a site.
evidence.page_or_section: Appendix A — Glossary of Terms, page 734

evidence.excerpt: Runoff Capture Volume (RCV). The runoff capture volume is equivalent to the water quality volume (WQV) and is the storm water runoff volume generated by the first inch of rainfall on the site.
evidence.page_or_section: Appendix A — Glossary of Terms, page 731

evidence.excerpt: The pond should contain a low-flow drain with an adjustable gate valve allowing for gradual discharge. Recommended drawdown is 24 hours.
evidence.page_or_section: Chapter 8, Wet Detention Ponds, Table 3, page 639

evidence.excerpt: The bottom of the bioretention area should be three feet or more above the seasonal high water table
Water table Bottom of the basin > 3 feet above the seasonal high water table depth
The bottom of the reservoir should be a minimum of three feet above any limiting layer (e.g., seasonal high water table, glacial till, bedrock).
A separation depth of three feet or more is usually sufficient.
Sand/Gravel Substrate Aeration and drainage for planting bed is provided by a 12 to 20- inch deep sand and/or gravel bed.
Minimum dimensions for a bioretention area are 10 feet wide by 20 feet long. Any system wider than 20 feet should be at least twice as long to evenly distribute the flow.
A ponding depth of six to nine inches is recommended.
Water is retained during storm events and released into the permanent pool over 12 to 48 hours.
evidence.page_or_section: Chapter 8, Wet Detention Ponds, Table 4, page 640

evidence.excerpt: Shallow Marsh. The portion of a storm water wetland that consists of aquatic vegetation within a permanent pool ranging in depth from 6 inches to 18 inches during normal conditions.
evidence.page_or_section: Appendix A — Glossary of Terms, page 731

extraction_quality.review_notes: Municipality coverage via Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual referenced by Evansville drainage code; local EMC may add site-specific criteria.

design_parameters.enrich_notes: Manual glossary defines WQV as runoff from one inch of rainfall; BMP sections often size treatment for small storms described as typically 0.5 to 1.5 inches (reservoir/first-flush language). SHWT separation of three feet appears consistently for infiltration, bioretention, wet ponds, wetlands, and porous pavement reservoirs. Bioretention ponding is recommended as six to nine inches (range, not a single design depth). Wet extended detention variant cites release over 12 to 48 hours; dry extended detention excerpt in corpus has no explicit drain time.
